title: Max Junestrand (Legora): Raising the bar in legal AI
author: Max Junestrand

dom.t: Legora expansion: Workflow usefulness must sustain global scale

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Junestrand describes a material shift from individual augmentation toward end-to-end agentic task execution, including partners assigning work directly to agents. This is relevant to the cluster’s premise that AI may redistribute associate work, but he does not address whether that shift undermines apprenticeship, creates a verification-expertise paradox, or requires reconstructed training.
qs: It's allowed to interact with knowledge sources with different skills, with other tools via MCP, and it's really  starting to move to becoming an end-to-end task multiplier instead of just an individual augmentation of a lawyer.
But now the partners are really starting to utilize it and to  give tasks directly to the agents cuz they know what they can expect in terms of outputs, and I think that's really exciting.

st.t: Harvey strategy: Prestige supports infrastructure ambitions
st.an: Junestrand presents LLMs as enabling broad legal-technology rebuilding, but provides no evidence or argument about Harvey’s prestige-led distribution, workflow-infrastructure ambitions, commercial traction, or governance-based copilot model. His account therefore does not establish a clear position on the cluster’s proposition.
qs: There are so  many solutions that will be rebuilt.
There are so many new things that you can now go and solve, which were impossible with the technology pre-LLMs.

st.t: Legora expansion: Workflow usefulness must sustain global scale
st.an: The interview introduction supports Legora’s rapid international and fundraising narrative, but it does not address whether workflow usefulness sustains that scale, nor provide evidence on product performance, legal-work improvement, partnerships or centralised engineering.
qs: You started the company not that long ago, but you've grown extremely fast.
You are now serving more than 40 markets.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Legora accepts the cluster’s application-layer thesis and materially develops it through a model-agnostic strategy, concentrated investment in priority legal workflows, rapid iteration with lawyers, and compliant shared infrastructure supporting bottom-up adoption. It does not, however, provide evidence on human verification or comparative performance.
qs: The models were so new and I think there was a lot of debate in the industry what the best course of action was and because we didn't have the funding and because we were the second mover, I think we just made a bet which was let's use every frontier model and let's build all of our functionality like boats so that when the tide rises, you know, everything improves.
And I think one of the superpowers that you have as a small team, and we definitely had in the beginning, and we're trying to keep very much now as we continue to grow, is this iteration cycle.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Junestrand accepts that organisational value depends on operating-model design rather than tool access alone, and materially extends the proposition with a concrete distributed model: compliant, scalable central infrastructure combined with AI capabilities embedded in individual functions. His bottom-up experimentation emphasis is somewhat broader than selective deployment, but remains grounded in governed organisational foundations and iterative reassessment as models improve.
qs: But, we sort of embed that AI capability across the different functions and then they get to use this central hub that is set up in a compliant and scalable way.
But, it's important then to set up all the building blocks so that they exist in a compliant and and good way.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Junestrand supports the proposition that AI is reorganising legal production rather than simply eliminating lawyers: Legora is moving from individual augmentation toward agents that execute broader tasks using firm context, while retaining a long-term model in which legal work is performed by people, machines or both. His account is more bullish on agentic delivery than the cluster’s emphasis on bounded automation, but he also identifies human adoption and implementation cycles as practical constraints.
qs: We are augmenting legal work with AI and we are building Legora to become the place where legal work happens either by a person or by a machine or together.
Because even if we can build things really quickly, the adoption and the implementation of that technology also needs to happen.

st.t: Startup scaling: Founder context can become bottleneck
st.an: Junestrand directly supports the cluster’s core proposition that scaling requires founders to move beyond personal problem-solving by hiring stronger specialists and coordinating their work. His emphasis on collective input and adaptive judgment also aligns with delegation and reduced dependence on constant founder intervention, though he does not establish these practices’ causal effects.
qs: My main job at this point and I'm sure you feel the same is or maybe you don't feel the same is to hire people smarter than myself, you know, in their craft.
And your job and or my job just becomes more and more to help orchestrate that that group.

st.t: Vendor strategy: Faster building cannot eliminate integration
st.an: Junestrand directly supports the cluster’s core distinction: AI enables faster product iteration and an application-layer strategy built around improving frontier models, but enterprise implementation and adoption remain governed by slower human and organisational cycles.
qs: Because even if we can build things really quickly, the adoption and the implementation of that technology also needs to happen.

The models were so new and I think there was a lot of debate in the industry what the best course of action was and because we didn't have the funding and because we were the second mover, I think we just made a bet which was let's use every frontier model and let's build all of our functionality like boats so that when the tide rises, you know, everything improves.

kp.k: LLMs create opportunities to rebuild legal software
kp.d: Junestrand characterises legal technology as a greenfield market in which LLMs enable previously impossible solutions and the rebuilding of existing products. He identifies access to GPT 3.5 in 2023 as the turning point for his co-founders' earlier AI-and-law experiments; this is a vendor founder's account of technological opportunity.
qs: What happened then was we got access to GPT 3.5 in 2023 and the world changed.
There are so many solutions that will be rebuilt. There are so many new things that you can now go and solve, which were impossible with the technology pre-LLMs.

kp.k: Embedded law-firm collaboration accelerated product development and adoption
kp.d: Junestrand describes working inside Mannheimer Swartling, putting the product directly into lawyers' hands after addressing security, compliance and data privacy questions, and iterating through informal demonstrations. He credits successful use cases with internal diffusion and the firm's endorsement with attracting other Nordic firms before wider expansion.
qs: So we actually got invited to work from within the firm.
We passed all the security and compliance and data privacy questions that they had.
And once we got a couple of successful use cases, that started spreading like wildfire in the firm.
So other firms were quick to follow.

kp.k: Application-layer investment leverages improving frontier models
kp.d: Junestrand says limited funding and second-mover status led Legora to use frontier models rather than pursue fine-tuning, concentrating on application capabilities such as larger document sets, web connectivity, Word drafting and document extraction. He contrasts this software-first approach with legacy information publishers' attempts to become software companies. A late-2024 memo prioritised three use cases, though the transcript names only two; he reports subsequently expanding to 10 product teams.
qs: let's use every frontier model and let's build all of our functionality like boats so that when the tide rises, you know, everything improves.
So, how do we make it possible to work with 100 documents and not just 10 documents?
Drafting in Word was one of them or running large document extractions was another.
now we have 10 product teams running at different things in parallel

kp.k: Early product failures can undermine lawyers' trust
kp.d: Junestrand argues that some early legal-AI entrants damaged adoption by exposing lawyers to inadequate products in early 2023. He attributes stronger trust in Legora's mid-2024 offering to improved functionality and describes a deliberate decision not to sell after raising $35 million. His statement that lawyers require perfection is a commercial judgement, not a measured reliability finding.
qs: And when a lawyer works with a tool, if it's not perfect, it's not good enough.
a lot of people tried AI back in early 2023 and they hated it.
after we had raised $35 million we said, "We are not going to sell."

kp.k: International expansion combines local law with anchor customers
kp.d: Junestrand describes integrating local case law and legislation and partnering with prominent firms or enterprises as prerequisites for entering markets. He cites CAM in India as an example of an anchor relationship generating wider interest. He says similar technology stacks across large enterprises and legal teams facilitate internationalisation, while rapid organisational growth creates communication challenges.
qs: when we go to a new market, the product has to be integrated with local legal knowledge. So, case law, legislation, et cetera.
And we need to partner with a winning brand and a winning firm and a winning enterprise.
when we went to India for instance, we did so with one of the top top law firms, CAM.
We went from 40 people to 400 in less than 12 months.

kp.k: Agentic systems extend beyond individual lawyer augmentation
kp.d: Junestrand describes a new agentic operating system that accesses firm context, knowledge sources, skills and other tools via MCP rather than simply responding to a query. He presents this as a move toward end-to-end task execution and adding agents to teams. This is a product-direction claim; the interview does not specify legal-output verification arrangements or establish unsupervised reliance.
qs: It's allowed to interact with knowledge sources with different skills, with other tools via MCP
it's really starting to move to becoming an end-to-end task multiplier instead of just an individual augmentation of a lawyer.
it really starts to feel like you're adding agents to your team rather than you yourself just being slightly faster because of it.

kp.k: Partners increasingly delegate tasks directly to agents
kp.d: Junestrand says associates were Legora's largest user group in 2025, using it for speed, improved work and an additional pair of eyes. He reports that partners are now using the technology directly and assigning tasks to agents because they understand expected outputs. This describes changing usage by seniority, not evidence of associate displacement or altered staffing ratios.
qs: In 2025, I'd say the biggest user group of Legarra was the associates.
But now the partners are really starting to utilize it and to give tasks directly to the agents cuz they know what they can expect in terms of outputs

kp.k: Customer expansion extends into tax, compliance and risk
kp.d: Junestrand identifies deeper legal workflows as Legora's primary expansion priority while reporting customer demand in adjacent tax, compliance and risk functions. He reports 300% net revenue retention last year among existing core customers; the transcript provides no calculation or supporting financial data.
qs: the most important thing for us is to go deeper in the vertical where we are already serving some of the biggest clients
we're getting pulled into adjacent areas like tax and we're starting to work with compliance and risk.
we drove a 300% net revenue retention last year.

kp.k: Human implementation constrains rapid technical iteration
kp.d: Junestrand regards quarterly product roadmaps as too slow for AI development but says enterprise customers still need a three-month view to plan implementation. He distinguishes software-building speed from professionals' capacity to change working practices and identifies the difficulty of innovating while simultaneously delivering professional work.
qs: I think quarterly is definitely too long for a product roadmap, but you need to know where you want to be a quarter from now.
the adoption and the implementation of that technology also needs to happen. And that's not being run at the cycle of an agent, that's being run at the cycle of a person.
it's very hard to be a professional and do the work at the same time as you are responsible for innovating the way that it's done.

kp.k: Customer study reports additional discoveries through AI
kp.d: Junestrand reports that a recent third-party return-on-investment study spoke with 30 of Legora's biggest clients and found that 71% of lawyers using Legora find things they otherwise would not. The transcript supplies neither the third party's identity nor respondent counts, methods or objective performance measures. He uses the reported finding to argue that foregoing AI is suboptimal and calls non-use in transaction data-room review almost unethical; this is his normative judgement, not a professional-rule requirement.
qs: We actually just recently did a big return on investment study by a third party who spoke with 30 of our biggest clients and found that 71% of all lawyers when they work with Legora, they find things they otherwise wouldn't have.
I would say it's almost unethical today to not leverage AI in reviewing the data room.
Because the AI will find things that a human will not.

kp.k: Engineering automation shifts constraints toward human verification
kp.d: As a cross-domain example inside Legora, Junestrand describes AI drafting code from reported bugs, running tests and routing pull requests through a review bot that determines whether human review is needed. He says few lines of code are now written manually and identifies engineers' capacity to review AI-generated code as a constraint. He wants to transfer engineering practices to other corporate functions; the example does not establish equivalent automation of legal work.
qs: there's very few lines of code being written manually at this point.
a bug comes in from Slack. That gets triaged in linear and then Cursor looks at it and makes a first PR.
And then a review bot looks at that PR and says if it's high security or low security and if a person needs to review it.
it does put a limit on the engineering team's ability to review a lot of the AI-generated code.

kp.k: Shared infrastructure supports distributed AI implementation
kp.d: Junestrand describes a central compliant, scalable functionality hub combined with AI operations embedded in individual departments, including a marketing engineer. He favours making capabilities accessible to curious employees over imposing adoption solely from the top. His broader organisational approach combines distributed decision-making, rapid reversible decisions and clear individual responsibilities.
qs: We have a central sort of functionality hub that is available to every team and then we are embedding AI operations in all of the teams.
marketing will have its own marketing engineer.
they get to use this central hub that is set up in a compliant and scalable way.
I think that's more important than a top-down decision of going, "Hey, we need more AI here."

kp.k: AI-native organisations avoid incumbent capacity dilemmas
kp.d: Junestrand argues that building a company around AI from the outset offers an advantage over introducing it into large existing teams. His illustrative 25% capacity-release scenario highlights uncertainty over what workers would then do and the resulting motivational problem. He also recommends revisiting unsuccessful AI applications as models improve; these are managerial observations rather than measured employment effects.
qs: a lot of the things that didn't work with AI now work as the models have improved.
I think that this is a real advantage that you have building a company today versus having a really big company and trying to scale that down
hey, let's implement AI and it's going to free up 25% capacity because then there's a question of well, what is that capacity now going to go and work on?

kp.k: Systems thinking becomes a central AI-era skill
kp.d: Junestrand recommends understanding the end-to-end system that produces work, rather than focusing exclusively on executing individual tasks, because this helps identify where AI fits. He also argues that learning to work with AI improves future professional prospects and emphasises curiosity and ambition in hiring. These are recommendations, not findings from a skills or labour-market study.
qs: learning the skills of working with AI today will set up you as a professional to be more successful in the future
I think it's process thinking or systems thinking or whatever you want to call it
what's the end-to-end process because if you can think about that, it's much easier to understand where AI will fit into it.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Junestrand claims LLMs open previously infeasible legal applications and create opportunities to rebuild existing legal technology.
pts.d: He describes legal technology as a largely greenfield opportunity following access to GPT-3.5 in 2023. Legora's strategy was to build an application layer on frontier models so that model improvements would improve its functionality, concentrating initially on workflows such as drafting in Word and large-document extraction. This is his account of product strategy and technological opportunity, rather than a quantified forecast of market replacement.

pts.k: Junestrand claims legal AI is moving from individual assistance toward agents performing end-to-end tasks, with partners increasingly assigning work directly.
pts.d: He contrasts query-and-response assistance with an agentic system that accesses firm context, knowledge sources, skills and other tools. He reports associates as Legora's largest user group in 2025 and describes a current shift toward direct partner use. His longer-term vision is a common environment for human work, machine work and collaboration. He does not explicitly predict lawyer headcount reductions or specify that agent outputs can be relied on without human verification.

pts.k: Junestrand claims AI-assisted review finds matters lawyers would otherwise miss, making non-use suboptimal and, in major transaction reviews, almost unethical.
pts.d: He presents improved issue detection as a benefit beyond speed. His statement about ethics is his own normative assessment, not a claim that a professional rule or court has established a duty to use AI. He extends the implication from transactional data-room review to working with AI on almost everything.

pts.k: Junestrand claims legal-AI adoption depends on product quality, human change capacity and local integration, while similar technology stacks support international expansion.
pts.d: He says disappointing early tools damaged lawyers' trust, whereas improved products won trust later. He describes local legal knowledge and partnerships with leading firms as conditions for entering new markets, with broadly similar enterprise legal technology stacks facilitating expansion. He also reports expansion within existing customers into tax, compliance and risk. These are vendor-market observations, not claims about ALSP delivery or a change in law-firm ownership.

pts.k: Junestrand predicts AI skills and systems thinking will enable small teams to accomplish more, while implementation and human review can constrain gains.
pts.d: This broader knowledge-work claim draws on Legora's internal operations rather than evidence of legal-sector staffing changes. He treats engineering as a model for other functions: AI generates code and automated systems triage it, but human review capacity becomes a constraint. He expects AI-skilled professionals to be more successful and identifies end-to-end process thinking as an important skill. The reference to freeing 25% capacity is a hypothetical management scenario, not a measured productivity result.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal quantitative support is a reported third-party client study; most other claims rely on Junestrand's founder experience and company-reported adoption.
pts.d: For improved issue detection, Junestrand cites a recent third-party ROI study that spoke with 30 of Legora's biggest clients and reports a 71% lawyer finding. The transcript does not name the third party, give the lawyer-level denominator, explain methods or provide a controlled comparison. His observations of partner use, successful workflows and international diffusion are experiential. He reports 300% net revenue retention for the preceding year as evidence of expansion within customers, not as a measure of legal accuracy or productivity. Early examples include adoption at Mannheimer Swartling and market interest following a partnership with CAM in India. No model benchmark or court case is offered.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The account distinguishes early limitations in 2023, improved adoption in 2024, associate-led use in 2025 and a current agentic transition; the longer-term vision has no fixed completion date.
pts.d: The document labels the interview 2026, making references to 'now' and 'today' current to that setting and 'last year' apparently 2025. Junestrand's agentic transition depends on models accessing firm context, knowledge and tools, and on partners understanding expected outputs. International adoption requires local legal integration and leading-client partnerships. He says technological development is faster than human implementation and that enterprise customers still require visibility three months ahead. The study is described only as recent; no study dates are supplied.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly affected groups are associates, partners, large law firms and enterprise legal teams, with adjacent corporate functions and legal-software suppliers also implicated.
pts.d: Associates use AI for speed, improvement and an additional check; partners increasingly delegate directly to agents. Transaction teams are said to gain issue-detection capability. Large law firms and enterprise legal departments are the main customer setting, while tax, compliance and risk represent adjacent uses. Junestrand portrays legacy legal information publishers as facing competition at the software application layer. His internal-company examples concern engineering, marketing, finance, HR and leadership. He does not make concrete predictions about access to justice, consumer legal services, billing models, associate promotion or legal employment losses.
